questions.prompt: What is the core mistake in regression to the mean?
choices: Treating a rebound after an extreme result as automatic proof that the latest action caused it
Assuming all improvement is random
Believing that interventions never matter

explanation.gentle: Yes. A move toward ordinary levels is getting overread as intervention proof.
explanation.direct: Correct. Ordinary reversion is being mistaken for strong causal effect.
explanation.competitive: That is the trap. The last touch steals the headline from the baseline.

questions.prompt: Why is this bias easy to believe?
choices: Because a clean before-and-after sequence feels like a satisfying causal story
Because extreme results always repeat at the same intensity
Because baseline variation is never relevant

explanation.direct: Correct. Dramatic swings invite neat causal stories.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. Drama hates leaving the baseline on stage.

questions.prompt: Which example best fits regression to the mean?
choices: A terrible month is followed by harsh feedback and then a more ordinary month, and the feedback gets full credit
A long-run improvement appears across many repeated observations after a new process is introduced
A score remains equally extreme across several trials

explanation.gentle: Yes. The rebound may partly reflect the extreme starting point easing.
explanation.direct: Correct. A single bounce from an extreme baseline is being overread as strong proof of the intervention.
explanation.competitive: That is it. The lecture is surfing a rebound that may already have been coming.

questions.prompt: What makes this bias dangerous in feedback systems?
choices: It can reward or punish the wrong cause after ordinary rebound from an extreme result
It proves that feedback should never be used
It means all performance variation is meaningless

explanation.gentle: Yes. People can learn the wrong lesson from one rebound.
explanation.direct: Correct. Praise or punishment can collect more credit than the evidence supports.
explanation.competitive: Right. Ordinary variation gets turned into management mythology.

questions.prompt: Why do extreme results often soften next time?
choices: Because part of what made them unusual often does not repeat with the same force
Because every next result is guaranteed to be average
Because any intervention always cancels the first result

explanation.gentle: Right. The unusual mix behind the extreme result often weakens.
explanation.direct: Correct. Extreme observations often include rare factors that are not fully repeated.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. The wild setup rarely shows up in the same costume twice.

questions.prompt: What is the practical correction in this chapter?
choices: Compare the rebound against what would likely happen after an extreme result anyway
Ignore all feedback after bad results
Assume the last intervention caused nothing at all

explanation.gentle: Yes. The fix is to compare the change against ordinary variation.
explanation.direct: Correct. Better judgment asks what expected reversion looks like before awarding causal credit.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. Make the baseline testify before the speech begins.

questions.prompt: What does regression to the mean confuse?
choices: Natural movement from an extreme result with strong proof that the latest action worked
Planning with memory
Routine with laziness

explanation.gentle: Right. Ordinary rebound is being treated as decisive intervention effect.
explanation.direct: Correct. Sequence is being mistaken for robust causal evidence after an extreme baseline.
explanation.competitive: Yes. The last touch hijacks a swing the baseline already loaded.

questions.prompt: Why can praise or punishment be misleading after an extreme outcome?
choices: Because some of the next change may have been likely even without the feedback
Because praise and punishment never affect behavior
Because all follow-up results are meaningless

explanation.gentle: Yes. The next result may have softened partly on its own.
explanation.direct: Correct. The extreme baseline can make a rebound look more causal than it really is.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. The lecture may be grabbing applause from gravity.

questions.prompt: What is the deepest practical correction in this bias?
choices: Use baseline variation and repeated comparisons before turning one rebound into a lesson
Assume every rebound is meaningless noise
Trust whichever explanation comes immediately after the swing

explanation.gentle: Yes. The chapter asks you to compare the story against ordinary variation first.
explanation.direct: Correct. Better judgment tests the rebound against broader evidence before claiming a strong cause.
explanation.competitive: Right. Put the baseline in the record before the legend gets printed.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's threshold question?
choices: Would some of this change likely have happened anyway because the starting point was extreme?
Which intervention sounds most convincing right now?
How dramatic was the rebound after the change?

explanation.gentle: Yes. That question brings the baseline back into view.
explanation.direct: Correct. It tests whether the change still looks special once expected reversion is considered.
explanation.competitive: That is the cut. Was the swing already half-loaded before the intervention showed up?
